pumac-2015-finals-a-01.title: Maximal placements are the boundary ones
pumac-2015-finals-a-01.body:
As in the Finals B problem, Alice has the maximum number $2(N-1)$ of bishops ($N=2015$), and equality in the counting bound forces every bishop to lie on the boundary of the board. (Each bishop must attack exactly $N-1$ squares, which happens only on the boundary.)

**Groups.** For $2\le i\le N-1$ the four boundary squares $(1,i),(i,1),(N,N+1-i),(N+1-i,N)$ form a group in which $(1,i),(i,1)$ share a diagonal, $(N,N+1-i),(N+1-i,N)$ share a diagonal, $(1,i),(N+1-i,N)$ share a diagonal and $(i,1),(N,N+1-i)$ share a diagonal. So at most $2$ squares of each group are used, and exactly $2$ in a maximum placement. There are exactly $2$ ways: $\{(1,i),(N,N+1-i)\}$ or $\{(i,1),(N+1-i,N)\}$. The corners form two more groups, $\{(1,1),(N,N)\}$ and $\{(1,N),(N,1)\}$, each contributing exactly one bishop, in $2$ ways. Squares of different groups do not attack each other. The total maximum is $2(N-2)+2=2N-2$ and the number of placements is $2^{N-2}\cdot2\cdot2=2^N$.

(Brute force for $N=3,4,5$ confirms $2^N$ maximal placements: $8,16,32$.)

So the number of ways is $2^{2015}$, i.e. $p_1=2$, $\alpha_1=2015$, and $\sum p_i+\alpha_i=2+2015=2017$.

**Answer: 2017**

pumac-2015-finals-a-03.title: Identify Y as the B-excenter
pumac-2015-finals-a-03.body:
**$ID=BD=AD$.** $\angle BID=\angle BCI+\angle CBI=\angle DBA+\angle ABI=\angle DBI$, so $ID=BD$ ($D$ is the midpoint of arc $AB$, so $DA=DB=DI$).

**Which side is the hypotenuse.** $DX>ID$ (as $X$ lies on the minor arc $AC$), and $XY<DX$ for $AB>BC$ (as in the figure), so the hypotenuse must be $DX$: $DX^2=ID^2+XY^2$.

**Key identity.** For $X$ on the arc, $DX^2-DA\cdot DB=AX\cdot BX$ (follows from similar triangles $ADF\sim DXF\sim BXD$ with $F=AX\cap$ tangent at $D$). Since $ID=DA=DB$, the condition becomes $AX\cdot BX=XY^2$.

**Locate $Y$.** $XY$ bisects the angle $AXB=\angle C$ (external side), so $\angle AXY=\angle BXY=180^\circ-\frac12\angle C$, and $\frac{AX}{XY}=\frac{XY}{BX}$ gives $\triangle AXY\sim\triangle YXB$. Hence $\angle AYB=\frac12\angle C$. If $BY$ meets $\omega_2$ again at $P$, then $\angle ACP=\angle AYP=\angle AYB=\frac12\angle C$, so $P$ lies on the bisector of $\angle C$; the bisector meets $\omega_2$ only at $C$ and $I$, so $P=I$. Thus $Y$ lies on line $BI$, and it is the $B$-excenter of $\triangle ABC$.

**Compute.** $\triangle BIA\sim\triangle BCY$ ($\angle ABI=\angle YBC$, $\angle BAI=\angle BYC$), so $\frac{BY}{BC}=\frac{BA}{BI}$ and $BY=\frac{20\cdot15}{12}=25$. Therefore $IY=BY-BI=25-12=13$.

**Answer: 13**
